title: Designing Human-Governed Contract Intelligence
subtitle: A Controlled Design-Science Evaluation of Authority-Aware Retrieval, Human Decision Rights, and Transaction Compliance
abstract: Develops and evaluates a human-governed contract-intelligence artifact that combines versioned evidence, semantic normalization, task-context retrieval, role-based access, accountable human decision rights, obligation activation, and deterministic transaction controls.
research_question: How should enterprise contract intelligence connect probabilistic interpretation and retrieval to authoritative, governed operational execution?
method: Design Science Research using a controlled synthetic benchmark of 36,000 clause records, 5,000 retrieval queries, and 20,000 transaction cases across two independent random seeds.
findings: The governed method achieved mean Hit@1 of 91.1% versus 12.6% for a semantic-only baseline, eliminated observed wrong-version retrieval and permission leakage within the benchmark, and produced 89.3% correct automated transaction decisions while abstaining on unresolved cases.
contribution: Positions contract intelligence as an end-to-end governed information system rather than a stand-alone language-model task, with explicit separation between evidence, authority, human decision rights, and transactional controls.
keywords: Contract intelligence; RAG; enterprise information systems; design science research; human-AI governance; transaction compliance

title: From Spend Visibility to Governed Spend Intelligence
subtitle: A Design Science Architecture for AI-Assisted Classification, Opportunity Discovery, and Finance-Validated Value
abstract: Develops a governed spend-intelligence artifact integrating supplier normalization, machine-learning classification, semantic spend modeling, opportunity detection, human review, and finance validation.
research_question: How should enterprise spend intelligence combine AI-based classification and opportunity discovery with governance controls so recommendations remain traceable, reviewable, and financially measurable?
method: Design Science Research using a controlled synthetic benchmark of 30,000 procurement transactions and 800 suppliers.
findings: The governed hybrid classifier achieved 95.9% accuracy and 0.959 macro-F1 versus 79.9% and 0.815 for a description-only baseline. High-confidence predictions achieved 100.0% accuracy on the held-out split while routing 35.9% of records for human review. Supplier alias normalization achieved 100.0% accuracy under controlled perturbations; opportunity detection remained the weakest component.
contribution: Connects AI classification to supplier resolution, confidence-based review, commercial opportunity detection, and finance-certified value realization rather than treating spend classification as an isolated model task.
keywords: Spend intelligence; procurement analytics; AI classification; supplier normalization; design science; human-AI governance

title: Enterprise AI as a Governed Operating Layer
subtitle: An Integrated Architecture for Context, Orchestration, Agentic Execution, and Systems-of-Record Integrity
abstract: Presents an integrated enterprise AI architecture spanning experience, orchestration, intelligence, context, systems/data, governance, and observability, with systems of record remaining authoritative.
research_question: How should enterprise architecture enforce authority in retrieval and gate agentic tool execution so AI can act without displacing authoritative data, permissions, workflow state, or accountable human decision rights?
method: Design Science Research with two controlled synthetic experiments: a 25,000-record knowledge corpus with 5,000 queries and a 10,000-scenario action-governance benchmark.
findings: Governed retrieval achieved 97.8% Hit@1 on authorized queries versus 52.0% for similarity-only retrieval and eliminated stale/non-authoritative exposure within the benchmark. Risk-based action controls reduced unsafe direct execution from 62.0% to 0.0%.
contribution: Defines where probabilistic reasoning belongs, where deterministic control must intervene, and how systems of record preserve transaction authority in agentic enterprise AI.
keywords: Enterprise AI; agentic AI; enterprise architecture; RAG; orchestration; systems of record; governance

title: From Periodic Scorecards to Continuous Supplier Risk Intelligence
subtitle: A Design Science Architecture for Multi-Signal Early Warning and Human-Governed Mitigation
abstract: Develops a governed supplier-risk intelligence artifact combining supplier identity, multi-signal feature engineering, explainable scoring, event correlation, analyst review, and mitigation workflow.
research_question: How should an enterprise system combine multi-signal supplier-risk analytics, business criticality, explainability, materiality controls, and human mitigation workflow?
method: Design Science Research using a synthetic panel of 2,500 suppliers over 18 monthly periods with a temporal train/test split.
findings: A financial-only baseline achieved ROC-AUC 0.909 and F1 0.803; the governed multi-signal model achieved ROC-AUC 0.998 and F1 0.987. The study explicitly treats these unusually clean synthetic results as a limitation and does not claim field performance.
contribution: Separates risk probability from supplier criticality and frames AI as a ranking/explanation layer while sourcing and risk professionals retain mitigation authority.
keywords: Supplier risk; supply chain resilience; early warning; explainable AI; procurement; human-AI governance

title: Governing AI-Assisted Purchase Order Generation
subtitle: A Design Science Architecture for Contract-Aware Drafting, Deterministic Validation, and Transaction-Safe ERP Execution
abstract: Develops a governed purchase-order architecture in which AI assists drafting and explanation while deterministic validation and authorized enterprise writes retain transaction authority.
research_question: How should AI-assisted PO generation preserve contract validity, supplier eligibility, accounting validity, pricing tolerance, approval authority, idempotency, and supplier dispatch control?
method: Design Science Research using a controlled synthetic benchmark of 25,000 PO scenarios.
findings: Unsafe PO creation fell from 15.5% to 0.0%, duplicate creation under retries from 1.8% to 0.0%, and incorrect supplier dispatch from 3.9% to 0.0% within the controlled benchmark. The study also measures the friction cost of deterministic gating.
contribution: Establishes a transaction boundary where AI output remains a draft until authoritative procurement and ERP controls validate and commit it.
keywords: Purchase order; procurement; generative AI; contract intelligence; ERP integration; idempotency; human approval

title: From Natural-Language Need to Governed ERP Requisition
subtitle: A Design Science Architecture for AI-Assisted Purchase Requisition Generation
abstract: Develops a governed AI-assisted requisition artifact that converts natural-language business need into structured ERP requisitions while preserving policy, budget, master-data, approval, and transaction integrity.
research_question: How should an AI-assisted requisition artifact combine natural-language understanding, retrieval, classification, deterministic validation, human review, and ERP creation without turning the model into a purchasing authority?
method: Design Science Research using 24,000 synthetic requisition requests with known category and control states.
findings: Category classification achieved 78.5% accuracy and 0.793 macro-F1. High-confidence predictions achieved 100.0% accuracy while routing 24.5% of requests for review. Unsafe ERP submission fell from 9.8% in an unrestricted baseline to 0.0% under governed controls within the benchmark.
contribution: Shows how AI can interpret and draft while deterministic services validate, accountable users approve, and ERP remains authoritative; it also introduces a targeted clarification-loop design for ambiguous fields.
keywords: Purchase requisition; procurement; NLP; RAG; ERP; human-in-the-loop; design science; enterprise AI

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Capital Projects: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Procurement and Competitive Bidding
abstract: Proposes a governed capital-project procurement architecture in which AI-assisted multi-criteria bid intelligence supports professionals while deterministic eligibility, conflict, sanctions, and approval controls remain authoritative.
research_question: Can AI-assisted multi-criteria bid intelligence improve decision support without bypassing mandatory procurement controls, and what false-block versus unsafe-selection trade-offs emerge?
method: Design Science Research using a reproducible 18,000-case synthetic bid benchmark.
findings: The benchmark evaluates governed versus ungoverned selection behavior under policy exceptions, missing/invalid data, and other failure modes. Results are treated as mechanism tests rather than field-deployment evidence.
contribution: Provides an auditable architecture for combining AI-assisted bid ranking with policy controls and accountable human award decisions.
keywords: Capital projects; procurement; competitive bidding; AI governance; decision support

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Capital Projects: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Purchase Order Generation and Transaction Control
abstract: Develops a governed architecture for AI-assisted PO preparation in capital projects, including exception handling, approval validation, idempotent ERP writes, committed-state verification, and supplier dispatch.
research_question: How should AI-assisted PO preparation be separated from authoritative ERP execution, and how do idempotency and committed-state validation affect integration failures?
method: Design Science Research using a reproducible 22,000-case synthetic PO benchmark plus integration-failure simulation.
findings: The governed policy achieved a 0.0000 duplicate rate and 0.0000 premature-dispatch rate in the controlled benchmark, with a 0.9473 success rate versus 0.9177 for the naive policy.
contribution: Extends governed AI into capital-project transaction execution with explicit recovery, idempotency, and committed-state controls.
keywords: Capital projects; purchase orders; ERP; idempotency; transaction governance

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Capital Projects: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Contract Management, Change Orders, and Compliance Intelligence
abstract: Proposes a governed contract and change-order intelligence architecture that separates probabilistic extraction/retrieval from authoritative document hierarchy, role authorization, delegation limits, and human approval.
research_question: How can contract/change-order intelligence respect document hierarchy and delegated authority, and how do authority controls alter wrong-version exposure and false blocking?
method: Design Science Research using a 16,000-case synthetic stress test with hidden exceptions and superseded-text conditions.
findings: Wrong-authority exposure fell from 0.2209 in the baseline to 0.0000 under governed controls, while the false-block population rate fell from 0.1003 to 0.0327.
contribution: Treats contract hierarchy and delegated authority as executable governance mechanisms rather than post-processing review.
keywords: Capital projects; contracts; change orders; NLP; authority; compliance

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Facilities Management: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Operations, Maintenance, Procurement, and Service Delivery
abstract: Presents a governed facilities-management architecture in which AI assists request classification, urgency prediction, knowledge retrieval, and service recommendations while deterministic policy and accountable operators govern work execution.
research_question: Can facilities-service requests be prioritized reproducibly from operational signals, and how should AI recommendations interact with safety, SLA, vendor, and dispatch controls?
method: Design Science Research using a 24,000-request synthetic benchmark comparing interpretable and ensemble urgency models.
findings: Logistic regression achieved ROC-AUC 0.9443 and F1 0.7906; random forest achieved ROC-AUC 0.9405 and F1 0.7799 on the controlled benchmark.
contribution: Connects predictive service prioritization with operational control boundaries across safety, vendor, SLA, and work-order execution.
keywords: Facilities management; work orders; maintenance; service delivery; AI governance

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Enterprise Asset Management: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Asset Lifecycle, Predictive Maintenance, Reliability, and Work Execution
abstract: Proposes a governed EAM architecture for asset-health interpretation, failure-risk prediction, maintenance prioritization, and human-controlled work execution.
research_question: How accurately can asset failure risk be estimated from multi-signal condition/history data, and how should predictive risk be converted into governed maintenance actions?
method: Design Science Research using a reproducible 26,000-event synthetic asset benchmark.
findings: Logistic regression achieved ROC-AUC 0.8337 and F1 0.5126; random forest achieved ROC-AUC 0.8198 and F1 0.5719 in the controlled benchmark.
contribution: Separates predictive maintenance evidence from deterministic safety, authorization, and system-of-record controls.
keywords: Enterprise asset management; predictive maintenance; reliability; failure prediction; AI governance

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Real Estate Location Intelligence: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Location Master Data, Data Quality, and Portfolio Decisions
abstract: Proposes a governed AI architecture for location entity resolution, duplicate detection, hierarchy validation, geospatial enrichment, cross-system reconciliation, and human stewardship.
research_question: Can AI improve location entity resolution and data-quality detection across real-estate hierarchies, and which corrections require deterministic validation and stewardship?
method: Design Science Research using a reproducible 20,000-record synthetic location benchmark.
findings: The AI-only method achieved 0.7178 accuracy, 0.7006 precision, and 0.9407 recall; governed rule-consistency checks reached 1.0000 on all three measures within the synthetic benchmark.
contribution: Frames location intelligence as an enterprise master-data governance problem rather than merely a geocoding task.
keywords: Real estate; location intelligence; master data; entity resolution; data quality

group: Capital Projects, Facilities & Real Estate Research
title: AI-Enabled Real Estate and Lease Accounting: A Governed Enterprise Architecture for Lease Intelligence, Financial Compliance, and Portfolio Decision-Making
abstract: Proposes a governed lease-intelligence architecture in which AI supports lease interpretation and portfolio decisions while authoritative lease records, accounting policies, controls, and accountable professionals govern financial execution.
research_question: How can AI support lease interpretation without becoming an accounting authority, and how should version, payment-schedule, and source-authority controls govern lease intelligence?
method: Design Science Research using a 15,000-case synthetic lease benchmark.
findings: The AI-only method achieved 0.8345 accuracy, 0.9651 precision, and 0.8267 recall; governed rule-consistency checks reached 1.0000 within the modeled benchmark. The paper explicitly does not treat this as a substitute for field/accounting validation.
contribution: Defines a governed separation between probabilistic lease interpretation and authoritative financial execution.
keywords: Real estate; lease accounting; lease intelligence; compliance; AI governance

title: What If Creating a Purchase Requisition Were as Simple as Saying What You Need?
subtitle: A business-facing article on governed AI-assisted procurement.
abstract: A practitioner article explaining a governed approach to AI-assisted purchase requisitions in which AI interprets and drafts, rules validate, humans govern, and ERP executes.
research_question: How can AI simplify the employee procurement experience without weakening enterprise controls?
method: Business-facing synthesis of the purchase-requisition research program and its controlled evaluation.
findings: Highlights the 24,000-request controlled benchmark, including 78.5% category-classification accuracy and 9.8% to 0.0% unsafe ERP submissions within the evaluated benchmark.
contribution: Translates the underlying research into a practical enterprise-management argument about separating AI flexibility from transaction authority.
keywords: Enterprise AI; procurement; ERP; generative AI; procure-to-pay; digital transformation
